      • cubicBezier

        public static Easing cubicBezier​(double x0,
                                 double y0,
                                 double x1,
                                 double y1)
        Creates a standard cubic Bézier easing function with start point (0,0) and end point (1,1).

        This matches the common CSS cubic-bezier(x0, y0, x1, y1) syntax used in transition-timing-function and animation-timing-function.

        Common examples:

        • ease: cubicBezier(0.25, 0.1, 0.25, 1.0)
        • ease-in: cubicBezier(0.42, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0)
        • ease-out: cubicBezier(0.0, 0.0, 0.58, 1.0)
        • ease-in-out:cubicBezier(0.42, 0.0, 0.58, 1.0)
        Parameters:
        x0 - x-coordinate of the first control point (typically in [0,1])
        y0 - y-coordinate of the first control point
        x1 - x-coordinate of the second control point (typically in [0,1])
        y1 - y-coordinate of the second control point
        Returns:
        a new CubicBezier easing instance

      • cubicBezier

        public static Easing cubicBezier​(double startY,
                                 double x0,
                                 double y0,
                                 double x1,
                                 double y1,
                                 double endY)
        Creates a cubic Bézier easing function with custom start and end Y values.

        This extended version allows easings that do not begin at 0 or end at 1, useful for animating properties with non-zero ranges or for step-like effects.

        The curve still progresses from time 0 → 1, but output values range from startY at t=0 to endY at t=1.

        Parameters:
        startY - y-value at time 0
        x0 - x-coordinate of the first control point
        y0 - y-coordinate of the first control point
        x1 - x-coordinate of the second control point
        y1 - y-coordinate of the second control point
        endY - y-value at time 1
        Returns:
        a new CubicBezier easing instance with custom Y bounds

      • linear

        public static Easing linear​(double... values)
        Creates a linear easing function, supporting multiple styles similar to CSS timing functions.

        This method provides a unified entry point for creating fast, linear-based easings:

        • No arguments or empty array: Standard linear from 0 to 1
        • Single value: Constant output (always returns that value)
        • Two values: Simple linear interpolation from startY to endY
        • Multiple paired values (x0, y0, x1, y1, ...): Piecewise linear with explicit stops (like CSS linear() function)

        When providing paired stops (4 or more values), the input must follow this format: 

         x0, y0, x1, y1, x2, y2, ..., xn, yn
        where:
        • Each x is a time position in the range [0.0, 1.0]
        • x values must be strictly increasing
        • The first x should ideally be 0.0 and the last 1.0 (automatically added if missing, using nearest y)
        • y is the output value at that time position

        This matches the behavior of the modern CSS linear() easing function, allowing precise control over timing without the computational cost of cubic Bézier solving.

        Parameters:
        values - the input values defining the easing behavior
        • 0 values: linear from 0 → 1
        • 1 value: constant easing returning that value
        • 2 values: linear from values[0] → values[1]
        • 4+ values (even count): explicit stops as x/y pairs
        Returns:
        an Easing instance: either Linear, ConstantEasing, or LinearPiecewise
        Throws:
        IllegalArgumentException - if paired stops are provided with an odd number of values or if x positions are invalid (out of [0,1] or not increasing) Simple linear (default): 
        
 Easing easing = TimeFunctions.linear(); // 0 → 1 over time
        Constant value: 
        
 Easing constant = TimeFunctions.linear(42.0); // always returns 42.0
        Custom linear range: 
        
 Easing ramp = TimeFunctions.linear(10.0, 100.0); // from 10 → 100
        CSS-style piecewise linear: 
        
 Easing custom = TimeFunctions.linear(
     0.0, 0.0,
     0.25, 0.8,
     0.75, 0.2,
     1.0, 1.0
 );
 // Fast acceleration, then deceleration — all with linear segments

      • bakeEasing

        public static Easing bakeEasing​(Easing easing,
                                int segments)
        Bakes any easing function into a high-performance LinearPiecewise approximation using a uniform number of segments.

        This is useful for converting computationally expensive easings (e.g., CubicBezier) into extremely fast piecewise linear versions that are visually nearly identical. Ideal for particle systems, UI elements with thousands of instances, or any scenario where the easing is evaluated many times per frame.

        The resulting LinearPiecewise has no iteration or root-finding overhead — just a binary search and linear interpolation.

        If the input easing is already a ConstantEasing, it is returned directly (no baking needed).

        Parameters:
        easing - the source easing function to bake
        segments - the number of evenly spaced samples along the curve (minimum 1). Higher values = more accurate approximation. Typical values: 8–32 (visually indistinguishable from original for most curves).
        Returns:
        a LinearPiecewise that closely matches the input easing

      • bakeEasing

        public static Easing bakeEasing​(Easing easing,
                                double... xPositions)
        Bakes any easing function into a high-performance LinearPiecewise approximation using explicitly specified x-positions (stops).

        This overload allows full control over where the curve is sampled. Useful for adaptive sampling (more points where the curve changes rapidly) or when matching exact CSS linear() stops.

        The provided xPositions are automatically:

        • Sorted
        • Clamped to [0.0, 1.0]
        • Used to evaluate the original easing at those exact times

        If the input easing is already a ConstantEasing, it is returned directly.

        Parameters:
        easing - the source easing function to bake
        xPositions - one or more time positions in [0.0, 1.0] where the curve should be sampled. Duplicates are ignored (due to sorting), and values outside [0,1] are clamped.
        Returns:
        a LinearPiecewise with stops at the requested x-positions
        Throws:
        IllegalArgumentException - if no xPositions are provided
